warmup.q: A Kafka listener receives 10,000 payment events a second and hands each one to a fixed thread pool that writes 2,000 a second to the ledger. What happens over the next few minutes?
options: The listener slows down to 2,000 a second on its own
The pool rejects the extra events with RejectedExecutionException
Events pile up in the pool's queue, about 8,000 more each second, until the heap runs out
Kafka stops delivering because the consumer group sees a slow member
warmup.why: Executors.newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue, so it never rejects and never pushes back. The listener returns at once, poll() keeps fetching, and nothing tells the producer to slow down. Kafka would slow down if the listener itself blocked, but handing off to an unbounded queue hides the slowness until memory runs out.

sections.h: Pull, push, and the consumer that drowns
sections.html:
There are two ways to move data from a producer to a consumer.

In pull, the consumer asks for the next item when it is ready: Iterator.next(), ResultSet.next(), KafkaConsumer.poll(). The consumer sets the pace. The cost is a waiting thread: while the next item isn't there yet, the consumer's thread sits and does nothing.

In push, the producer calls the consumer when an item exists: a listener, a callback, CompletableFuture.thenAccept. Nobody waits. The cost is that the producer sets the pace, and the consumer has no way to say "slow down".

Push breaks when the producer is faster than the consumer. Here is a shape that shows up in payment services:

Java
// the listener returns at once, so the poll loop keeps fetching
void onMessage(PaymentEvent e) {
    ledgerWriter.execute(() -> ledger.write(e));   // a fixed pool: its queue has no limit
}
Kotlin
// the listener returns at once, so the poll loop keeps fetching
fun onMessage(e: PaymentEvent) {
    ledgerWriter.execute { ledger.write(e) }       // a fixed pool: its queue has no limit
}

Kafka itself is pull, and this code turns it into push. The listener returns in microseconds, so poll() keeps fetching, and the executor's LinkedBlockingQueue grows. With 10,000 events a second coming in and 2,000 going out, the heap gains 8,000 objects every second. Nothing fails at first. Then the garbage collector runs all the time, latency climbs, and the pod is killed for running out of memory.

Backpressure is the fix: the consumer tells the producer how much it can take, and the producer never sends more. Reactive Streams makes this part of the protocol. The subscriber calls request(n), and the publisher may then push at most n items. If items are ready, they arrive at once, as with pull. If they aren't, the publisher pushes them when they appear, as with push. The Reactor docs call this a push-pull hybrid.

When the consumer can't keep up, a system has four honest options: slow the producer down, buffer up to a limit, drop items, or fail. An unbounded queue is a fifth option that only looks like a choice. Reactive Streams makes you pick one of the four on purpose. Lesson 7 of this track, "Backpressure in practice", shows how to pick in Reactor.

try.title: Drown a ledger writer, then rescue it
steps: Read DrowningDemo below. It sends 100,000 events to a writer that needs 10 microseconds per event, first with plain push and then through a SubmissionPublisher with request(1).
Predict for each version: how long will the producer take, and how many events will be waiting in memory when it finishes?
Run it (Java or Kotlin, they print the same). Then change writeToLedger to wait 20,000 nanoseconds and run again. Which number changes in each line?

code.title: DrowningDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l01; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Flow; import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** A fast producer and a slow ledger writer, first with plain push, then with demand. */ public class DrowningDemo { static final int EVENTS = 100_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { pushWithoutDemand(); pushWithDemand(); } // Plain push: the producer hands every event to the writer's executor. Its queue has no limit. static void pushWithoutDemand() throws Exception { ExecutorService writer = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); AtomicLong written = new AtomicLong(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < EVENTS; i++) { writer.execute(() -> { writeToLedger(); written.incrementAndGet(); }); } long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; long w = written.get(); System.out.printf("plain push: producer done in %,5d ms, ledger wrote %,6d, %,6d events waiting in memory%n", ms, w, EVENTS - w); writer.shutdownNow(); } // With demand: the writer asks for one event at a time. submit() blocks when the 256-slot buffer is full. static void pushWithDemand() throws Exception { AtomicLong written = new AtomicLong(); long maxLag = 0; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (SubmissionPublisher<Integer> publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<>()) { publisher.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<Integer>() { Flow.Subscription s; public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { this.s = s; s.request(1); } public void onNext(Integer event) { writeToLedger(); written.incrementAndGet(); s.request(1); } public void onError(Throwable t) { t.printStackTrace(); } public void onComplete() { } }); for (int i = 0; i < EVENTS; i++) { publisher.submit(i); // waits while the buffer is full maxLag = Math.max(maxLag, publisher.estimateMaximumLag()); } long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; long w = written.get(); System.out.printf("with demand: producer done in %,5d ms, ledger wrote %,6d, never more than %,d waiting%n", ms, w, maxLag); } TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(50); } // stands in for a 10-microsecond ledger write static void writeToLedger() { long until = System.nanoTime() + 10_000; while (System.nanoTime() < until) Thread.onSpinWait(); } }

alt.title: DrowningDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.reactive.l01 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Flow import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong private const val EVENTS = 100_000 /** A fast producer and a slow ledger writer, first with plain push, then with demand. */ fun main() { pushWithoutDemand() pushWithDemand() } // Plain push: the producer hands every event to the writer's executor. Its queue has no limit. private fun pushWithoutDemand() { val writer = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() val written = AtomicLong() val t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(EVENTS) { writer.execute { writeToLedger(); written.incrementAndGet() } } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 val w = written.get() println("plain push: producer done in %,5d ms, ledger wrote %,6d, %,6d events waiting in memory".format(ms, w, EVENTS - w)) writer.shutdownNow() } // With demand: the writer asks for one event at a time. submit() blocks when the 256-slot buffer is full. private fun pushWithDemand() { val written = AtomicLong() var maxLag = 0L val t0 = System.nanoTime() SubmissionPublisher<Int>().use { publisher -> publisher.subscribe(object : Flow.Subscriber<Int> { private lateinit var s: Flow.Subscription override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) { this.s = s; s.request(1) } override fun onNext(event: Int) { writeToLedger(); written.incrementAndGet(); s.request(1) } override fun onError(t: Throwable) = t.printStackTrace() override fun onComplete() {} }) for (i in 0 until EVENTS) { publisher.submit(i) // waits while the buffer is full maxLag = maxOf(maxLag, publisher.estimateMaximumLag().toLong()) } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("with demand: producer done in %,5d ms, ledger wrote %,6d, never more than %,d waiting".format(ms, written.get(), maxLag)) } TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(50) } // stands in for a 10-microsecond ledger write private fun writeToLedger() { val until = System.nanoTime() + 10_000 while (System.nanoTime() < until) Thread.onSpinWait() }

try.expect: With plain push the producer finishes in tens of milliseconds and almost everything is still queued (one run here: 40 ms, 1,347 written, 98,653 waiting). With demand the producer takes as long as the writer needs (1,805 ms here) and never more than about 256 events wait, which is the publisher's buffer. With a 20 microsecond write, the plain version leaves even more events queued, and the demand version simply takes about twice as long. Its memory stays flat.

sections.h: Reactive Streams: the contract in seven methods
sections.html:
Reactive Streams is a small spec: four interfaces, seven methods, and a list of numbered rules. Here is all of the API:

Java
public interface Publisher<T>    { void subscribe(Subscriber<? super T> s); }
public interface Subscriber<T>   { void onSubscribe(Subscription s);
                                   void onNext(T item);
                                   void onError(Throwable t);
                                   void onComplete(); }
public interface Subscription    { void request(long n); void cancel(); }
public interface Processor<T, R> extends Subscriber<T>, Publisher<R> { }
Kotlin
// the same four interfaces, written as Kotlin declarations
interface Publisher<T>    { fun subscribe(s: Subscriber<in T>) }
interface Subscriber<T>   { fun onSubscribe(s: Subscription)
                            fun onNext(item: T)
                            fun onError(t: Throwable)
                            fun onComplete() }
interface Subscription    { fun request(n: Long); fun cancel() }
interface Processor<T, R> : Subscriber<T>, Publisher<R>

Every method returns void (Unit in Kotlin), so every call is a one-way message. Java's Subscriber<? super T> is Kotlin's Subscriber<in T>: a publisher of payments also accepts a subscriber of any supertype, such as a Subscriber<Object> that logs everything. A subscriber sees signals in one fixed order, which the spec writes as onSubscribe onNext* (onError | onComplete)?. That means one onSubscribe, then any number of onNext, then at most one terminal signal. After onError or onComplete, nothing else arrives.

You will rarely write these by hand. Reactor, RxJava, Mutiny (the library behind Quarkus' reactive APIs) and the reactive database drivers all implement them, and the rules are why one library can subscribe to another. The rules you will actually meet:

  • 1.1 A publisher never sends more onNext signals than were requested in total.
  • 1.3 Signals to one subscriber are serial: never two at the same time. So a subscriber needs no locks for its own fields.
  • 1.9 onSubscribe comes before any other signal.
  • 2.13 Subscriber methods must return normally. The only exception allowed is a NullPointerException for a null argument. A subscriber that wants to stop must call cancel(), not throw. An exception from onNext lands in the publisher's delivery code, which can't hand it back to the subscriber, so the spec has the publisher treat the subscription as cancelled and report the error some other way, such as a log line.
  • 2.8 A subscriber must accept onNext calls that arrive after it cancelled. Items already requested may still be on their way.
  • 3.9 request(n) with n <= 0 must produce onError(IllegalArgumentException).
  • 3.17 Demand of Long.MAX_VALUE may be treated as "unbounded". That is a subscriber saying it wants no backpressure at all.

Rule 3.9 is a good place to see that the spec and a library can differ. The JDK's publisher follows it. Reactor's operators only log a bad request at DEBUG level and send nothing, so a broken subscriber just waits forever. A stream that silently stalls is the symptom to remember.

try.title: Break rule 3.9 on purpose
steps: RequestZeroDemo has a subscriber that calls request(0) in onSubscribe. It subscribes to a JDK SubmissionPublisher and to a Reactor Flux.range(1, 3).
Predict what each publisher sends back. Then run it.
Change request(0) to request(2). Predict again: does each stream complete?

code.title: RequestZeroDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l01; import reactor.adapter.JdkFlowAdapter; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import java.util.concurrent.Flow; import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** A subscriber that breaks rule 3.9 by calling request(0). Two publishers react differently. */ public class RequestZeroDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (SubmissionPublisher<Integer> jdk = new SubmissionPublisher<>()) { jdk.subscribe(new Rude("JDK SubmissionPublisher")); jdk.submit(1); } TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(300); Flow.Publisher<Integer> reactor = JdkFlowAdapter.publisherToFlowPublisher(Flux.range(1, 3)); Rude rude = new Rude("Reactor Flux.range"); reactor.subscribe(rude); TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(300); if (!rude.signalled) System.out.println("Reactor Flux.range: no signal at all, the stream just stalls"); } static final class Rude implements Flow.Subscriber<Integer> { final String name; volatile boolean signalled; Rude(String name) { this.name = name; } @Override public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { s.request(0); } // rule 3.9 says: must be > 0 @Override public void onNext(Integer item) { signalled = true; System.out.println(name + ": onNext " + item); } @Override public void onError(Throwable t) { signalled = true; System.out.println(name + ": onError " + t); } @Override public void onComplete() { signalled = true; System.out.println(name + ": onComplete"); } } }

alt.title: RequestZeroDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.reactive.l01 import reactor.adapter.JdkFlowAdapter import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import java.util.concurrent.Flow import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** A subscriber that breaks rule 3.9 by calling request(0). Two publishers react differently. */ fun main() { SubmissionPublisher<Int>().use { jdk -> jdk.subscribe(RudeSubscriber("JDK SubmissionPublisher")) jdk.submit(1) } TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(300) val reactor: Flow.Publisher<Int> = JdkFlowAdapter.publisherToFlowPublisher(Flux.range(1, 3)) val rude = RudeSubscriber("Reactor Flux.range") reactor.subscribe(rude) TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(300) if (!rude.signalled) println("Reactor Flux.range: no signal at all, the stream just stalls") } private class RudeSubscriber(private val name: String) : Flow.Subscriber<Int> { @Volatile var signalled = false override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) = s.request(0) // rule 3.9 says: must be > 0 override fun onNext(item: Int) { signalled = true; println("$name: onNext $item") } override fun onError(t: Throwable) { signalled = true; println("$name: onError $t") } override fun onComplete() { signalled = true; println("$name: onComplete") } }

try.expect: The JDK publisher follows rule 3.9 and prints onError java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: non-positive subscription request. Reactor prints nothing at all: the stream just stalls. With request(2), the JDK publisher sends its one item and then onComplete, because it was closed. Reactor sends 1 and 2 and then stops without completing, because nobody asked for 3. Unmet demand never times out by itself.

refs.title: Reactive Streams for the JVM: specification and rules

video.title: Reactive Streams demand: the publisher sends only what the subscriber asked for

sections.html:
Java 9 copied the four interfaces into the JDK as nested types of java.util.concurrent.Flow: Flow.Publisher, Flow.Subscriber, Flow.Subscription and Flow.Processor. Same methods, same rules, different package. Reactor works with org.reactivestreams.Publisher, so you bridge with JdkFlowAdapter (in reactor-core) or FlowAdapters (in the reactive-streams jar).

The JDK ships one real implementation, SubmissionPublisher. You hand it items from ordinary code, and it delivers them to each subscriber asynchronously:

Java
try (var publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<PaymentEvent>()) {
    publisher.subscribe(new BatchingSubscriber<>(32, ledger::write));
    for (PaymentEvent e : events) {
        publisher.submit(e);       // blocks while this subscriber is 256 items behind
    }
}   // close(): subscribers get onComplete after their buffered items
Kotlin
SubmissionPublisher<PaymentEvent>().use { publisher ->
    publisher.subscribe(BatchingSubscriber(32, ledger::write))
    for (e in events) {
        publisher.submit(e)        // blocks while this subscriber is 256 items behind
    }
}   // close(): subscribers get onComplete after their buffered items

The parts that matter:

  • Each subscriber gets its own buffer. Its maximum size defaults to Flow.defaultBufferSize(), which is 256.
  • Delivery runs on an Executor. On JDK 21 the default is ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). Pass your own executor for anything slow.
  • submit(item) blocks the producer's thread when a subscriber's buffer is full. This is where backpressure turns into something an ordinary thread can feel. In the first Try it, submit is what slowed the producer down to the ledger writer's pace.
  • offer(item, onDrop) never blocks. When a buffer is full it calls your drop handler, and returns a negative number for each drop. There is also an offer with a timeout.
  • If a subscriber method throws, the publisher cancels that subscription.
  • close() completes every subscriber. closeExceptionally(t) sends them onError(t).

Blocking in submit is fine on a dedicated producer thread or a virtual thread. It is a bad idea on an event-loop thread (one thread that serves many connections, as the next section explains), where it stalls everything else on that loop.

SubmissionPublisher is a good teaching tool and a decent in-process fan-out, but it has no operators. You can't map, retry or time out a Flow.Publisher without writing the code yourself. That is the job Reactor does, starting with lesson 2 of this track.

try.title: Fill a two-slot buffer
steps: SaturationDemo builds a SubmissionPublisher with a buffer of 2 and a subscriber that never calls request. It then offers 10 items.
Predict what each offer returns and how many items are dropped. Run it.
Now replace the offer(...) call with publisher.submit(i) and keep the assignment to lag. Predict, then run it. Stop it with Ctrl+C.

code.title: SaturationDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l01; import java.util.concurrent.Flow; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** A SubmissionPublisher with a 2-slot buffer and a subscriber that never asks for anything. */ public class SaturationDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("default buffer: " + Flow.defaultBufferSize()); AtomicInteger dropped = new AtomicInteger(); try (SubmissionPublisher<Integer> publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<>(ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), 2)) { publisher.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<Integer>() { public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { } // never calls request(n) public void onNext(Integer item) { System.out.println("got " + item); } public void onError(Throwable t) { } public void onComplete() { } }); for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) { // offer() does not block. When the buffer is full it calls the drop handler instead. int lag = publisher.offer(i, (subscriber, item) -> { dropped.incrementAndGet(); return false; // false: don't retry, drop it }); System.out.printf("offer(%d) -> %d%n", i, lag); } System.out.println("dropped " + dropped.get() + " of 10, lag " + publisher.estimateMaximumLag()); } } }

alt.title: SaturationDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.reactive.l01 import java.util.concurrent.Flow import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** A SubmissionPublisher with a 2-slot buffer and a subscriber that never asks for anything. */ fun main() { println("default buffer: ${Flow.defaultBufferSize()}") val dropped = AtomicInteger() SubmissionPublisher<Int>(ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), 2).use { publisher -> publisher.subscribe(object : Flow.Subscriber<Int> { override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) {} // never calls request(n) override fun onNext(item: Int) = println("got $item") override fun onError(t: Throwable) {} override fun onComplete() {} }) for (i in 1..10) { // offer() does not block. When the buffer is full it calls the drop handler instead. val lag = publisher.offer(i) { _, _ -> dropped.incrementAndGet() false // false: don't retry, drop it } println("offer($i) -> $lag") } println("dropped ${dropped.get()} of 10, lag ${publisher.estimateMaximumLag()}") } }

try.expect: The first two offers return a lag of 1 and 2. Offers 3 to 10 each return -1, the drop handler runs eight times, and the last line is dropped 8 of 10, lag 2. Nothing is delivered, because nothing was requested. With submit the program hangs on item 3: the buffer is full, the subscriber never asks for more, and submit waits for space. That hang is backpressure reaching your thread.

sections.h: What non-blocking buys you, and what it costs
sections.html:
Here is what blocking IO costs. A thread sends a request to the card issuer and waits 120 ms for the answer. During those 120 ms it holds about a megabyte of stack and does no work. A pool of 200 such threads can have 200 calls in flight. By Little's law that caps you at 200 / 0.12 s, about 1,670 calls a second, however idle the CPUs are.

Non-blocking IO removes the wait. An event-loop thread (Netty, or the JDK's NIO selectors) hands the request to the operating system and moves on to other work. When the response bytes arrive, the loop runs a callback to continue. A handful of threads can keep thousands of calls in flight. Reactive libraries are the programming model for that callback world: a Mono is the one reply you are waiting for, a Flux is a stream of them, and demand travels with the data.

It has real costs. The Spring Framework docs say it plainly: "Reactive and non-blocking generally do not make applications run faster." The gain is "the ability to scale with a small, fixed number of threads and less memory", and you only see it when calls have latency. You also pay with stack traces that show operator internals instead of your code, a learning curve the whole team has to climb, and one strict rule: nothing on an event loop may block. A single JDBC call on an event-loop thread stalls every request that loop serves.

Virtual threads (JDK 21, JEP 444) changed the trade. A blocked virtual thread unmounts from its carrier, so blocking code no longer burns a platform thread per call. For request and response over JDBC, a plain blocking style on virtual threads is now the simpler default. Reactive still earns its place where the problem is a stream: backpressure, cancellation that travels upstream, rate-limited fan-out, retries and timeouts as composable operators. Lesson 8 of this track comes back to this choice with the Spring team's own words.

Quick check: your service makes 3,000 issuer calls a second, and each waits 120 ms. How many calls are in flight at any moment, and how many threads does each model need for them? (Little's law gives 3,000 x 0.12 s = 360 calls in flight. Blocking IO needs 360 threads, one parked per call. An event loop needs a handful, because no thread waits for a reply.)

refs.title: Spring Framework reference: WebFlux overview (applicability and performance)

analogy: Think of a kitchen and a waiter. With plain push the kitchen sends out every plate the moment it is cooked, and the waiter stacks them on a side table that keeps getting longer. With pull the waiter walks to the pass and stands there until a plate is ready. Reactive Streams is the waiter saying "I can carry three": the kitchen sends up to three plates, at once if they are ready or as soon as they are, and never a fourth until the waiter asks again. The analogy breaks at the end of the shift: a real kitchen notices when the waiter quits, but a publisher only stops when the subscriber calls cancel().
world: Your Kafka consumers already pull, which is why a slow listener slows poll() and eventually triggers a rebalance. The danger is the moment you hand records to something that doesn't push back: an unbounded executor queue, a CompletableFuture.runAsync per record, or a reactive pipeline that calls request(Long.MAX_VALUE). The same applies to a Temporal activity that streams settlement rows into an in-memory list, or a Quarkus endpoint that relays an issuer's event stream to clients. Ask one question of each: when the next stage is slow, what makes the stage before it wait?
mistake: The most common mistake is asking for everything. subscription.request(Long.MAX_VALUE) in onSubscribe, or a Reactor subscribe(item -> ...) with no demand control, tells the publisher "no backpressure, please". People do it because it is the shortest code that works in a test with ten items. In production the slow stage then buffers without limit or drops data. Request a bounded batch and ask for more as you finish, as in the lab.

compare.title: A one-at-a-time Flow.Subscriber in Java and Kotlin

java.title: OneAtATime.java
java.html: publisher.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<Payment>() { private Flow.Subscription s; public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { this.s = s; s.request(1); // ask for the first item } public void onNext(Payment p) { ledger.write(p); // slow work s.request(1); // only now ask for the next } public void onError(Throwable t) { log.error("feed failed", t); } public void onComplete() { log.info("feed done"); } });

kotlin.title: OneAtATime.kt
kotlin.html: publisher.subscribe(object : Flow.Subscriber<Payment> { private lateinit var s: Flow.Subscription override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) { this.s = s s.request(1) // ask for the first item } override fun onNext(p: Payment) { // non-null type: Kotlin itself throws NPE on null ledger.write(p) // slow work s.request(1) // only now ask for the next } override fun onError(t: Throwable) = log.error("feed failed", t) override fun onComplete() = log.info("feed done") })

compare.note: The protocol code is the same in both languages; three Kotlin details change how it feels. lateinit var s replaces the nullable field you would otherwise check. object : Flow.Subscriber<Payment> is Kotlin's anonymous class. And because onNext(p: Payment) declares a non-null parameter, the Kotlin compiler adds a null check to it: a publisher that sends null gets a NullPointerException, which is exactly what rule 2.13 asks for, with no code from you. Don't confuse java.util.concurrent.Flow with kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow. The Kotlin one is a coroutine stream with no request(n) at all: emit suspends until the collector has finished with the item, so a producer can never run ahead. The Spring docs call Kotlin Flow push-based and Reactor's Flux a push-pull hybrid. The coroutines track covers Flow, and kotlinx-coroutines-reactive converts between the two with asFlow() and asPublisher().

worked.title: Find the rule violations in a hand-written subscriber

steps.say: A teammate wrote this subscriber for a statement export. It reads rows from a reactive database driver and writes them to a file. Read it and look for broken rules before reading on.
steps.code: class ExportSubscriber implements Flow.Subscriber<Row> { private Flow.Subscription s; public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { this.s = s; s.request(Long.MAX_VALUE); } public void onNext(Row row) { if (row.amount() == null) throw new IllegalStateException("bad row " + row.id()); file.append(row.toCsv()); } public void onError(Throwable t) { s.request(1); } // "try again" public void onComplete() { file.close(); } }

alt.html: class ExportSubscriber : Flow.Subscriber<Row> { private lateinit var s: Flow.Subscription override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) { this.s = s s.request(Long.MAX_VALUE) } override fun onNext(row: Row) { if (row.amount == null) throw IllegalStateException("bad row ${row.id}") file.append(row.toCsv()) } override fun onError(t: Throwable) = s.request(1) // "try again" override fun onComplete() = file.close() }

steps.say: Three problems. request(Long.MAX_VALUE) turns backpressure off (rule 3.17), so a slow disk makes the driver buffer rows. Throwing from onNext breaks rule 2.13: the publisher may cancel, log, or do something you didn't expect. And calling request from onError breaks rule 2.3: after a terminal signal the subscription is dead.
Fix them one by one. Ask for one item at a time. Turn a bad row into a cancel plus a recorded error. Treat onError as the end.
steps.code: class ExportSubscriber implements Flow.Subscriber<Row> { private Flow.Subscription s; private boolean stopped; volatile Throwable failure; public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { this.s = s; s.request(1); // 1. bounded demand } public void onNext(Row row) { if (stopped) return; // 2. rule 2.8: late items may still come if (row.amount() == null) { stopped = true; failure = new IllegalStateException("bad row " + row.id()); s.cancel(); // 3. stop by cancelling, never by throwing return; } file.append(row.toCsv()); s.request(1); // 4. ask for the next one when done } public void onError(Throwable t) { failure = t; file.close(); } // 5. terminal: just clean up public void onComplete() { file.close(); } }

alt.html: class ExportSubscriber : Flow.Subscriber<Row> { private lateinit var s: Flow.Subscription private var stopped = false @Volatile var failure: Throwable? = null override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) { this.s = s s.request(1) // 1. bounded demand } override fun onNext(row: Row) { if (stopped) return // 2. rule 2.8: late items may still come if (row.amount == null) { stopped = true failure = IllegalStateException("bad row ${row.id}") s.cancel() // 3. stop by cancelling, never by throwing return } file.append(row.toCsv()) s.request(1) // 4. ask for the next one when done } override fun onError(t: Throwable) { failure = t; file.close() } // 5. terminal: just clean up override fun onComplete() = file.close() }

steps.say: This is correct but chatty: one request(1) call per row. Each call crosses into the publisher, and some publishers do real work per request. The lab asks for the same correctness with demand in batches, which is what Reactor's own operators do internally.

lab.title: A Flow.Subscriber that asks in batches
steps: Run the tests once. All five fail with TODO errors, and the two SubmissionPublisher tests also time out after 3 seconds.
Write onSubscribe: keep the subscription and call request(batchSize). If a subscription is already stored, cancel the new one and return.
Write onNext: reject null, pass the item to the handler, count it, and call request(batchSize) again only when a whole batch has been handled.
Make a throwing handler safe: catch it, cancel the subscription, record the error, count down done, and ignore any later onNext.
Write onError and onComplete so await returns. Run the tests until all five pass.
hints: You need two more fields: an int counting items in the current batch, and a boolean that says you have cancelled. Signals are serial (rule 1.3), so plain fields are safe here.
The request test expects exactly [4, 4, 4] for 10 items in batches of 4. If you see eleven requests, you are asking after every item. If you see [4], you never reset the counter.
Objects.requireNonNull(item) is all rule 2.13 asks for on null.

drill.title: Write a one-at-a-time subscriber from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a Flow.Subscriber<String> that requests one item at a time, prints each item, and cancels the subscription (without throwing) at the first item that starts with "ERR". Then compare with the answer. Did you guard against items that arrive after the cancel?

answer.html: class StopAtError implements Flow.Subscriber<String> { private Flow.Subscription s; private boolean stopped; public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { this.s = s; s.request(1); } public void onNext(String item) { if (stopped) return; // rule 2.8 if (item.startsWith("ERR")) { stopped = true; s.cancel(); // rule 2.13: cancel, don't throw return; } System.out.println(item); s.request(1); } public void onError(Throwable t) { t.printStackTrace(); } public void onComplete() { System.out.println("done"); } }

alt.html: class StopAtError : Flow.Subscriber<String> { private lateinit var s: Flow.Subscription private var stopped = false override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) { this.s = s s.request(1) } override fun onNext(item: String) { if (stopped) return // rule 2.8 if (item.startsWith("ERR")) { stopped = true s.cancel() // rule 2.13: cancel, don't throw return } println(item) s.request(1) } override fun onError(t: Throwable) = t.printStackTrace() override fun onComplete() = println("done") }

recap: Pull lets the consumer set the pace but parks a thread while it waits. Push never waits but lets a fast producer drown a slow consumer.
Backpressure means the consumer says how much it can take (request(n)) and the producer never sends more (rule 1.1).
Signals arrive as onSubscribe onNext* (onError | onComplete)?, one at a time. Subscribers stop by calling cancel(), never by throwing.
java.util.concurrent.Flow is the same contract in the JDK. SubmissionPublisher.submit blocks the producer when a subscriber's 256-item buffer is full; offer drops instead.
Reactor ignores request(0) silently, while the JDK reports it as onError. A stream with unmet demand just stalls.
Non-blocking IO scales with few threads when calls have latency. It does not make code faster, and virtual threads now cover plain request and response well.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why the payments team bothers with request(n) when "a queue in between does the same job". Explain in your own words what demand gives you that an unbounded queue doesn't, and when a queue is fine.
explain.answer: An unbounded queue lets the producer run as fast as it likes. When the consumer falls behind, the queue grows until the heap runs out, and nobody upstream finds out until the pod dies. With request(n) the consumer says how many items it can take, and the publisher may not send more. The slowness travels back to the producer: it blocks, buffers up to a limit, drops on purpose, or fails, and you choose which. A queue is fine when it is bounded and you have decided what happens when it is full (block the producer or reject), because then it is backpressure too. Kafka's poll loop is the same idea: the consumer pulls only what it can handle.

deeper.html:
Three details that will help later.

Why request takes a long. Demand adds up. A subscriber may call request(5) and then request(10) before any item arrives, and the publisher then owes 15. Rule 3.17 says a subscription must support demand up to Long.MAX_VALUE, and that total demand at or above 2^63 - 1 may be treated as unbounded. Reactor's subscribe(Consumer) uses exactly that: it requests Long.MAX_VALUE. Operators like limitRate and flatMap then turn that unbounded demand into bounded requests upstream, which is lesson 7 of this track.

Rule 3.3 and reentrancy. request may be called from inside onNext (rule 3.2), and a synchronous publisher may respond by calling onNext again from inside that request (rule 3.10). Done naively, a stream of a million items becomes a stack a million frames deep. Rule 3.3 makes publishers bound that recursion, usually with a small trampoline loop. This is one reason writing a correct publisher is much harder than writing a subscriber, and why you should use a library's.

The TCK. The Reactive Streams project ships a Technology Compatibility Kit: a set of tests that check a publisher or subscriber against the numbered rules. Library authors run it. Reactor's TestPublisher (lesson 8 of this track) borrows the idea for application tests: you can create a deliberately non-compliant publisher, for example one that ignores demand, and check that your code survives it.

Processor. A processor is both a subscriber and a publisher, so it can sit in the middle of a chain. Reactor used to expose processors directly. It has phased them out in favour of Sinks, which you'll meet in lesson 8 of this track.
